title: Mr C & The Health Service Executive (the HSE)
text:
Decision
Mr C & The Health Service Executive (the HSE)
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-161187-L6K1M5
Published on 9 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether the HSE was justified in its decision to refuse to confirm or deny, under section 37(6) of the FOI Act, the existence of records that mention the applicant
9 July 2026
Background
This review has its background in a previous decision this Office issued on 9 July 2025 in Case OIC-159213, wherein we annulled a decision of the HSE to refuse the applicant’s request under section 15(c) of the Act on the basis that it did not first properly comply with the provisions of section 15(4) of the FOI Act before doing so. We directed the HSE to process the request afresh.
The request was for all mentions of the applicant in any form (including variations of name and generic job title) by all staff in the hospital where he had worked as well as in his particular unit. He also specifically requested the same information from the accounts of 20 named individuals, including the CEO of the HSE. He requested all relevant records for the period 2 June 2023 to 12 February 2025.
On 22 July 2025, the HSE issued a fresh decision, wherein it refused the request under section 37(6)(b) of the Act. It said it considered that the disclosure of the existence or nonexistence of records may involve the disclosure of personal information relating to an individual or individuals other than the requestor which is prohibited under sections 37(1) and 37(7) of the FOI Act.
On 22 July 2025, the applicant sought an internal review of that decision. On 29 July 2025, the HSE issued its internal review decision wherein it affirm the original decision to refuse the request. On 5 August 2025, the applicant sought a review by this Office of that decision.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the correspondence outlined above, and to the correspondence between this Office and both parties on the matter. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
This review is concerned solely with whether the HSE was justified in its decision to refuse the applicant’s request for records that mention him under section 37(6) of the FOI Act.
Analysis and Findings
Section 37(1) of the FOI Act provides for the mandatory refusal of a request where the FOI body considers that granting access to the record sought would involve the disclosure of third-party personal information. Under section 37(6), where the FOI body considers that the disclosure of the existence or non-existence of the record sought would involve the disclosure of third-party personal information, it must refuse to grant the request and shall not disclose to the requester whether or not the record sought exists. Section 37(6) contains what is commonly referred to as a ‘neither confirm nor deny’ provision. It provides for the refusal of a request for access to a record and for the refusal to disclose whether or not such a record exists, provided the requirements of the subsection are met. The overall purpose of section 37(6) is to protect the personal information of a third party in situations where knowledge of the existence, or non-existence, of particular records would effectively disclose that party’s personal information. The usefulness of the provision depends upon it being invoked both in instances in which relevant records do not exist as well as in cases in which relevant records do exist.
Consideration of section 37(6) must be conducted on the basis of what would be the case were the FOI body to hold records of the kind sought by the requester, rather than on whether or not such records are actually held. For section 37(6) to apply, the following requirements must be satisfied:
• the record sought must be of a type which would disclose third-party personal information if it existed, and which would be exempt from release by virtue of section 37(1) of the FOI Act;
• none of the exceptions to the section 37(1) exemption, contained at subsections (2) or (5) of section 37, applies or, in the case where relevant records do not exist, would apply if such records did exist, and
• the FOI body must form the opinion that to state whether or not relevant records exist would, in itself, disclose third party personal information.
The question of whether confirming the existence or non-existence of relevant records would, in itself, disclose third party personal information generally depends on the nature of the records sought and on the manner in which the request has been framed.
In this case, the applicant essentially sought any records referencing him, either specifically, or by way of generic job title of the role he had held. I fully accept that it is possible that certain such records, if they exist, could contain third-party personal information. It is also possible that they could include nothing more than records created by the applicant’s colleagues in the course of the performance of their functions. On this point, I note that for the purposes of the FOI Act, where an individual holds or held a position as a member of the staff of an FOI Body, personal information does not include the name of the individual or information relating to the position or its functions or the terms upon and subject to which the individual occupies or occupied that position, or anything written or recorded in any form by the individual in the course of and for the purpose of the performance of his or her functions. Disclosure of the existence or non-existence of records coming within the scope of the request as framed in this case would disclose nothing more than the fact that the HSE either holds records that reference the applicant or it doesn’t. I fail to see how the disclosure of the existence or non-existence of such records, of itself, could possibly involve the disclosure of third-party personal information. If relevant records exist, disclosure of that fact discloses nothing about the contents of such records other than the fact that records exist that mention the applicant. Accordingly, I find that the HSE’s decision to refuse to confirm or deny the existence of relevant records pursuant to section 37(6) was not justified.
I would add, in any event, that by refusing the request in the first instance under section 15(1)(c) as it did in Case OIC-159213 (which provides for the refusal of a request where the FOI Body considers that granting the request would cause a substantial and unreasonable interference with or disruption of work of the FOI body concerned by reason of the number or nature of the records concerned), it seems to me that the HSE essentially indicated that it does, indeed, hold relevant records. This makes the HSE’s decision to rely on section 37(6) in its fresh consideration of the request rather strange.
As I have found that the HSE has not justified its decision to refuse to confirm or deny the existence of relevant records on the basis of section 37(6), and in order to preserve the HSE’s rights of appeal, I consider that I have no appropriate alternative other than to yet again remit the matter back to the HSE for consideration afresh.
The effect of this is that the HSE must, for a second time, consider the applicant’s request afresh and make a new, first instance decision in accordance with the provisions of the FOI Act. The applicant will have a right to internal review and a review by this Office if he is not satisfied with the HSE’s fresh decision. In the event that the applicant feels the need to apply to this Office for a further review, we will endeavour to prioritise any such review. I would also caution the HSE that pursuant to section 22(12)(b) of the FAOI Act, a decision to refuse to grant an FOI request is presumed not to have been justified unless the FOI body concerned can satisfy the Information Commissioner that its decision was justified. As such, if the matter appears before this Office again and the HSE fails to satisfactorily justify its decision, it runs a strong risk of records it considers exempt being released.
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act, I hereby annul the HSE’s decision to refuse the applicant’s request under section37(6) of the FOI Act and I direct it to carry out a fresh decision-making process on the request.
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
Stephen Rafferty
Senior Investigator
